03.actor: Rabbi Ami and a man claiming another man is a priest
03.event: A man came before Rabbi Ami asserting that another man had established a presumption of priesthood, because he was called first to read the Torah.
03.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether the first reading reflected priesthood or mere prominence, and the man answered that a Levite read after him.
03.outcome: Rabbi Ami accepted the statement and elevated the man to the priesthood.
03.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami and said another man had shown himself to be a priest by reading the Torah first in the synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether he read first because he was a priest or because he was a great man. The witness answered that a Levite read after him, which only happens when a priest reads first. Rabbi Ami accepted this and elevated the man to the priesthood.

05.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a man vouching for another's Levite status
05.event: A man came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi claiming another man was a Levite because he was called to read second in the synagogue.
05.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi pressed whether second reading showed Levite status or mere prominence, and the man answered that a priest had read before him.
05.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted the statement and elevated the man to Levite status.
05.summary: A man came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and said another man was shown to be a Levite because he read second in the synagogue. Rabbi Yehoshua asked whether that was because of Levite status or because of prominence. The man replied that he was certain, since a priest had read before him. Rabbi Yehoshua accepted this and elevated the man to Levite status.

08.event: Captive women redeemed in Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's upper room with the ladder removed, and he was seized by desire for one of them and climbed a huge ladder alone.
08.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself and cried out that there was a fire in Amram's house, bringing the Sages to see him.
08.outcome: He said it was better to be shamed in this world than the next, adjured his evil inclination to leave him as a pillar of fire, and told it that he, flesh, was greater than it, fire.
08.summary: Captive women who had been redeemed were put up in Rav Amram the Pious's house, with the ladder removed from their attic. One was so beautiful that light seemed to shine from the opening, and Rav Amram, desiring her, lifted a ladder ten men could not carry and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and cried out that there was a fire in his house, so the Sages came and saw him. He told them it was better to be shamed in this world, then made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire and declared that flesh had beaten fire.

10.actor: Ameimar and a woman claiming one-tenth of her father's estate
10.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for a tenth of her father's estate, and her brothers said that if they had cash they would pay her off with it.
10.turn: Ameimar stayed silent rather than objecting to the brothers' offer.
10.outcome: Rav Minyumi took the silence to show Ameimar had retracted and now saw the daughter as a creditor who can be paid in money.
10.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers said that if they had the money they would pay her off in cash, and Ameimar said nothing. Rav Minyumi read this silence as Ameimar's retraction of his earlier view.
10.missing: The passage is mostly a legal dispute with the anecdote serving as evidence; no actual ruling in the woman's case is given.

11.actor: Rav Nahman, judging between a creditor and a herdsman of orphans' cattle
11.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive, while the herdsman said it was after death.
11.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses that the creditor seized it, and he had none.
11.outcome: Rav Nahman reasoned that since the creditor could claim he purchased it, he could equally claim he seized it during the debtor's life, so the creditor's claim stands.
11.summary: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, saying he took it while the father was alive. The herdsman said it was after the father's death, and they came before Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether he had witnesses to the seizure, and he said no. Rav Nahman reasoned that the creditor could just as well have claimed to have bought the ox, so he is believed that he seized it during the debtor's lifetime.

12.actor: Rava and Rav Natan bar Ami
12.event: Rava coerced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity and collected four hundred dinars from him.
12.outcome: Rava collected four hundred dinars for charity from him against his will.
12.summary: Rava once compelled the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give to charity and took four hundred dinars from him. It is cited as proof that a wealthy man can be forced to give, and so can be forced to support his children.
12.missing: No detail of how the incident unfolded or Rav Natan's reaction; it is a one-line precedent.

13.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, who had to pay daily medical costs for their father's widow, asked him what to do, and he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
13.turn: Rabbi Yohanan later regretted it, saying they had made themselves like legal advisors.
13.outcome: The text explains he first followed the verse about not hiding from one's own flesh but concluded an important person should not do this.
13.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had their father's wife on their hands, needing treatment every day. They came to him and he advised them to fix a lump sum with the doctor, which would turn the cost into a deduction from her marriage contract. Later he said in regret that they had made themselves like legal advisors, since at first he had thought it right to help relatives but ultimately held that an important person should not.

14.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rava and his father Rava
14.event: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study with Rav Yosef for six years, and on the eve of Yom Kippur after three years the son decided to go home to see his wife.
14.turn: Rava heard, took a weapon and went to meet him, rebuking him for remembering his mistress or dove.
14.outcome: Father and son were so upset by the argument that neither ate the pre-Yom Kippur meal.
14.summary: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study for six years in the study hall. Three years in, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son said he would go see his family. Rava heard, took a weapon and went out to meet him, asking whether he had remembered his mistress, or by another version his dove. They were so preoccupied by the clash that neither ate the cessation meal.

16.event: The court of priests set a marriage contract for virgins and widows, saw widows being demeaned and raised the widow's sum to two hundred.
16.turn: They saw that men were avoiding widows of priests and marrying Israelite virgins instead.
16.outcome: They restored the widow's amount to its original level.
16.summary: Priestly courts first set a marriage contract of four hundred dinars for a virgin and one hundred for a widow. Seeing priests demean widows, they raised the widow's sum to two hundred. Then they saw men were avoiding priestly widows to marry Israelite virgins at the same cost, so they restored the original amount.
16.missing: This is a stylized account of legal history by a collective actor, not an anecdote with specific people or a dated event.

18.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha and the matter of whether an eiruv was needed came before the Sages.
18.outcome: The Sages ruled that only the place where he actually lives renders carrying prohibited.
18.summary: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha, only one of which he lived in. The case was brought before the Sages to decide whether an eiruv was required for all. They ruled that only a place of residence imposes a prohibition.
18.missing: It is a bare precedent report with no characters' actions or reactions beyond the ruling.

19.event: The Sages asked Rabbi Abbahu to show them where Rabbi Elai was hiding, and he answered with a cryptic wordplay sentence.
19.turn: His answer was a riddle, which can mean either that Elai was kept awake by a young wife or by a priestly tractate.
19.outcome: Abbahu's answer is understood as saying Elai is sleeping after a sleepless night.
19.summary: The Sages asked Rabbi Abbahu where Rabbi Elai was, and he replied with a riddle. It is explained either as a young priestly wife who kept him awake or a challenging tractate he studied all night. Either way, Elai is sleeping.
19.missing: The scene is a single riddling exchange with no development, and the answer's meaning is supplied by commentary.

20.actor: Rava, a divorced betrothed couple, and Rav Adda bar Mattana
20.event: A man and woman whose betrothal was dissolved came before Rava over repayment, and Rava had an intermediary placed between them.
20.turn: Rav Adda bar Mattana objected, citing Rav Nahman that a betrothal divorcee is paid directly, and was answered that this couple appeared accustomed to each other.
20.outcome: Rava's separation of the couple stood, with a second version having Rav Adda urge the separation and Rava objecting.
20.summary: A divorced betrothed couple came before Rava, who placed an intermediary between them. Rav Adda bar Mattana objected that a woman divorced from betrothal is paid directly. Rava replied that the rule applies only to those not accustomed to each other, and he saw that these two were. In a second version the roles are reversed, with Rav Adda urging the separation and Rava citing the rule.
